guides.title: How to Validate a Business Idea
guides.summary: A practical, evidence-first method for testing whether a business idea will work before committing money and years to it: finding the assumption that would kill you, running customer interviews and demand experiments that can genuinely fail, proving the unit economics and the channel, and deciding honestly whether to persevere, pivot or stop.

sections.heading: The Expensive Habit of Building First
sections.body:
The most common way to lose money and years on a business is not to execute badly. It is to execute well on something nobody wanted. Post-mortems collected from failed startups, most famously the running analysis published by CB Insights, put "no market need" at or near the top of the list of stated causes, cited in something like a third to forty percent of failures. That figure should be read with caution, since founders write their own post-mortems and hindsight is a poor witness, but the direction is consistent across every source that has looked. The dominant failure mode is building a solution to a problem that was not painful enough, for people who were not willing to pay, in a way they could not be reached.

Validation is the discipline of finding this out cheaply and early, before the money and the years are committed. It is not market research in the traditional sense of surveys and focus groups, though those have their place. It is a sequence of deliberately designed, deliberately cheap experiments, each aimed at the specific belief that would do the most damage if it turned out to be wrong. The mental shift is from "how do I build this?" to "what would have to be true for this to work, and how do I test the shakiest of those things this week?"

The economics of the shift are stark. A serious software product takes six to eighteen months and, at market salaries, easily two hundred thousand to two million pounds or dollars to build. A landing page with a paid traffic test costs a few hundred and takes a weekend. A set of thirty customer interviews costs nothing but three weeks of persistent effort. If a handful of experiments in that price range can tell you that the idea is wrong, the saving is not marginal; it is the difference between a bad month and a lost decade.

There is an important caveat that honest treatments acknowledge. Validation reduces risk, it does not eliminate it, and it is not a guarantee. Plenty of ideas that validated poorly went on to succeed, because the founder was testing the wrong hypothesis or reaching the wrong people. Airbnb, Slack and Uber all faced early evidence that would have discouraged a rigid interpretation of the data. Conversely, plenty of ideas that produced encouraging early signals collapsed later. What validation reliably does is kill obviously bad ideas fast, sharpen ambiguous ones, and force the founder to make their assumptions explicit enough to be argued with. That is a large benefit even though it is not certainty, and the discipline is worth practising precisely because the alternative, building on unexamined belief, has such a well-documented failure rate.

sections.heading: What Validation Actually Means, and What It Does Not
sections.body:
Validation has been diluted by overuse into a vague synonym for "checking that people like the idea." Used properly it has a precise meaning: it is the process of testing a specific, falsifiable belief about the world by gathering evidence that could genuinely come out the other way. The last clause is the one people skip. If no realistic outcome of your test would cause you to abandon or change the plan, you have not run a validation experiment. You have run a reassurance exercise.

The distinction is easiest to see in what gets counted as evidence. Someone saying "that sounds like a great idea" is not evidence. Neither is a friend saying they would definitely use it, a survey respondent ticking "very interested," or a LinkedIn post attracting a hundred likes. All of these cost the respondent nothing, and things that cost nothing reveal nothing about behaviour under cost. Real evidence involves the other party giving up something they value: money, time, reputation, data, or access. A signed letter of intent is evidence. A pre-order with a card charged is stronger evidence. Someone taking forty-five minutes out of a working day to walk you through their current painful process is meaningful evidence about the pain. A verbal compliment is noise.

Two ideas from the wider literature anchor this. Steve Blank, whose Four Steps to the Epiphany in 2005 largely founded the customer development movement, is best known for the instruction to get out of the building: no facts exist inside your office, only opinions. Eric Ries built on that in The Lean Startup in 2011 with the build-measure-learn loop and the concept of validated learning, learning that is demonstrated by data from real customers rather than asserted. Both frameworks have since been criticized, fairly, for encouraging a mechanical box-ticking approach and for suiting some businesses far better than others, but their central claim has held up well.

It is equally important to be clear about the limits. Validation cannot tell you whether a genuinely novel product will create a market that does not yet exist; customers cannot report on preferences they have never had the chance to form. It cannot substitute for taste and judgment in categories driven by aesthetics or culture. It is weak for very long sales cycles, for regulated industries where the binding constraint is legal rather than commercial, and for deep technology where the dominant risk is whether the thing can be built at all. In those cases the shape of the process changes: you validate feasibility and regulatory pathway first, and commercial demand later. Recognizing which risk dominates your particular idea is the first real decision, and getting it wrong means running beautifully designed experiments on the question that was never going to kill you.

sections.heading: Finding the Assumption That Would Kill You
sections.body:
Every business idea is a stack of beliefs, most of them invisible to the person holding them. A plan to sell a scheduling tool to independent physiotherapists contains, at minimum, beliefs that independent physiotherapists exist in sufficient number, that scheduling causes them meaningful pain, that they perceive that pain, that they are not already adequately served, that they have authority to buy, that they will pay a price above your cost to serve, that you can find and reach them affordably and repeatedly, that they will keep paying, and that nothing legal or technical blocks you. Any one of these being false can end the business. Most founders test the one they find most interesting rather than the one that is most likely wrong and most fatal.

The remedy is a written assumption inventory, and the writing matters because unarticulated beliefs cannot be examined. List every belief the plan depends on, phrased as a declarative statement that could be true or false. Vague statements are useless here: "physiotherapists need better software" cannot be tested, whereas "at least a third of solo physiotherapists spend more than three hours a week on scheduling admin and describe it unprompted as a top-three frustration" can be.

Then rank the list on two axes. The first is importance: if this belief were false, would the business be dead, wounded, or merely inconvenienced? The second is uncertainty: how much real evidence do you actually have, as opposed to how confident you feel? These come apart constantly. Founders are frequently very confident about the things they have never checked, usually because those beliefs come from their own experience and feel like facts. The assumptions to test first are the ones scoring high on both axes: fatal if wrong, and genuinely unknown. This ordering is sometimes called the riskiest assumption test, and it is the single highest-leverage habit in the whole discipline.

A useful discipline is to write the pre-mortem before running anything. Imagine it is two years from now and the business has failed. Write the story of why, in specific terms. This technique, developed by the psychologist Gary Klein and popularized in decision-making research, reliably surfaces risks that forward-looking planning misses, because it licenses pessimism that optimistic planning suppresses. The failure stories people generate this way are usually accurate; the problem was never ignorance, it was that nobody had asked the question in a form that made saying it socially acceptable.

Expect the inventory to change. Every experiment you run answers one assumption and typically exposes two new ones you could not have seen before. This is a sign the process is working rather than a failure of planning. The list is a living document, and its main value is preventing you from drifting into building while the fatal question sits unexamined.

sections.heading: The Three Risks: Desirability, Viability, Feasibility
sections.body:
A structure that has proved durable, associated with the design consultancy IDEO and with Tim Brown's articulation of design thinking, sorts the risks in any new venture into three families. It is worth learning because it stops you from concentrating all your effort on one flank while another collapses.

Desirability asks whether anybody wants this. Is there a real problem, is it painful enough that people are already spending money, time or ingenuity trying to solve it, and does your proposed solution actually relieve that pain in their eyes rather than yours? This is the risk that customer interviews, smoke tests and pre-sales address, and it is the one most commonly fatal in consumer and small-business products. The tell-tale signal of a desirability failure is polite interest that never converts into behaviour.

Viability asks whether the numbers work. Even if people want it, can you sell it at a price above what it costs to make and deliver, acquire customers for less than they are worth over their lifetime, and retain them long enough to recover that acquisition cost? A product can be genuinely loved and still be a bad business, and this happens far more often than founders expect. Meal-kit delivery, on-demand home services and many consumer subscription categories are littered with companies that had enthusiastic customers and unrecoverable unit economics. Viability failures tend to appear later than desirability failures, which makes them more expensive, so they deserve testing earlier than instinct suggests.

Feasibility asks whether you can actually build and operate it, with the technology that exists, the skills and capital you can assemble, and within the law. For most software businesses feasibility is the least of the three risks, because the technology is well understood and the constraint is really execution. For hardware, biotechnology, novel materials, anything involving medical claims, financial services, or handling of regulated data, feasibility can dominate everything else, and the correct sequence inverts: you establish that the thing can legally and physically be done before you spend heavily on demand testing.

The practical instruction is to identify which of the three is your binding constraint and attack it first, rather than defaulting to the one you enjoy. Engineers reflexively work on feasibility because building is comfortable and talking to strangers is not. Salespeople reflexively work on desirability and discover the margin problem eighteen months in. Finance-trained founders build elaborate viability models for demand that was never verified to exist.

A fourth risk is increasingly added to the list and deserves mention: adaptability or defensibility, meaning whether the business can survive competitive response and change. This one is genuinely hard to test in advance and is more a matter of strategic judgment than experiment, which is an honest limitation rather than something to paper over with a framework.

sections.heading: Customer Discovery Interviews: The Core Skill
sections.body:
Talking to prospective customers is the foundational technique, and it is harder than it looks because the default conversation produces flattering, useless answers. The purpose of a discovery interview is not to describe your idea and gauge enthusiasm. It is to understand the person's current situation in enough detail that you can judge for yourself whether a real problem exists, how they handle it now, what that handling costs them, and whether they have ever spent money on it.

Aim for volume and spread. Fewer than about fifteen conversations and you are reading noise; the useful patterns generally start emerging somewhere between twenty and forty, at which point new interviews stop surprising you. That saturation point is the signal to stop. Talk to people you do not know, because friends and family systematically flatter, and to a range of situations rather than only the ones that confirm the story. Deliberately seek out people who tried something like your solution and abandoned it, since they know exactly why it did not work.

Structure each conversation around the past rather than the future. Ask when they last encountered the problem, what specifically happened, what they did about it, how long it took, what it cost, and what they tried before. Memory of concrete recent events is reasonably reliable; predictions of future behaviour are not. Record or take verbatim notes, because paraphrase silently launders their words into your framing, and the exact phrasing customers use is itself commercially valuable later for marketing copy.

The three signals that matter most are whether the problem surfaces without prompting, whether they have already built a workaround, and whether money has already moved. A spreadsheet someone maintains by hand every Friday evening is worth more than any stated preference, because it is behaviour under cost. Workarounds in particular are the most reliable single indicator in the whole method: nobody builds and maintains a clumsy manual process for a problem that does not genuinely hurt, and the effort they have already sunk into it is a direct measure of how much the pain is worth to them.
ingredients: A written list of ten to fifteen open questions about the person's current process, none of which mention your solution

A recruiting source: industry association directories, trade groups, LinkedIn search, relevant subreddits and forums, professional bodies, conference attendee lists, or introductions from anyone already in the sector
A short honest outreach message that asks for help understanding their work rather than offering a demo, which reliably gets a far higher response rate
A recording tool with explicit permission asked at the start, or a second person taking verbatim notes
A simple shared spreadsheet or document with one row per interview, capturing quotes, current workarounds, money already spent, and whether the problem came up unprompted
A modest incentive where appropriate, such as a twenty-five to fifty pound or dollar gift card, which is standard for consumer research and usually unnecessary for business interviews

sections.heading: Asking Questions That Yield Truth Instead of Flattery
sections.body:
The single most useful practical text on interviewing is Rob Fitzpatrick's short book The Mom Test, published in 2013. Its premise is that you should be able to ask questions so well constructed that even your mother, the person most motivated in the world to be kind to you, could not lie to you. The way to achieve that is to never mention your idea, and to ask only about facts in the other person's life rather than opinions about yours.

Three rules carry most of the weight. Talk about their life instead of your idea. Ask about specifics in the past instead of generics about the future. Talk less and listen more. Once you describe your idea the conversation is contaminated, because the other person now knows what answer would please you and most people will oblige. Save the pitch for the end, if at all.

Contrast the question forms directly. "Would you use an app that tracked your invoices?" invites a costless yes. "Walk me through how you handled your last three overdue invoices" produces a story with real detail in it. "Do you think this is a good idea?" solicits an opinion the person is unqualified to give. "How much did that mistake cost you last time it happened?" produces a number. "Would you pay fifty pounds a month for this?" is a hypothetical everyone answers optimistically. "What are you currently paying for anything in this area?" is a matter of record.

Learn to recognize the compliments and hedges that feel like progress and are not. "That's really interesting," "I would definitely buy that," "let me know when it launches," and "you should talk to my colleague about it" are all pleasant and all worthless. Fitzpatrick calls this fluff. The correct response is to press for the concrete: when did you last have this problem, what did you do, what did it cost, who else was involved, what would need to be true for you to change what you do now.

The strongest close available is asking for a commitment right there, calibrated to how early you are. That might be a follow-up meeting with the budget holder, an introduction to two colleagues, permission to observe them working for an hour, agreement to trial a prototype next month, or an actual deposit. Each of these costs the other person something real, and their willingness to pay that cost is the measurement. Someone who loves the idea but will not spend twenty minutes making an introduction has told you the truth regardless of what they said. Treat the pattern of refused commitments as your primary dataset rather than an awkward footnote.

sections.heading: Sizing the Market Without Fooling Yourself
sections.body:
Market sizing is where optimistic arithmetic does the most damage, because a large number in a slide deck feels like evidence when it is usually just multiplication. The standard vocabulary distinguishes three nested figures. The total addressable market, TAM, is the annual revenue if every conceivable buyer on earth bought from you. The serviceable addressable market, SAM, narrows to the segment you can actually reach given your geography, language, channel and product. The serviceable obtainable market, SOM, is the realistic share you could win in the next few years given competition and your own capacity.

The dangerous method is top-down: find an industry report claiming the global wellness market is worth five trillion, assume you capture one percent, and announce a fifty billion opportunity. This is arithmetic dressed as analysis. Those headline figures are usually drawn from vendor-sponsored research with elastic category boundaries, the one percent is arbitrary, and no business in history has ever won share by assuming it.

The honest method is bottom-up, built from countable units. Establish how many potential buyers exist, using sources you can actually check: government business registries, census and labour statistics, professional licensing bodies, trade association membership counts, company filings, app store rankings, job postings as a proxy for team sizes. Multiply by a defensible price derived from what comparable things already cost, and by a realistic penetration rate. Then show your working so somebody can attack each number individually.

A worked example makes the discipline concrete. Suppose the product is scheduling software for solo physiotherapists in the United Kingdom. The professional register lists on the order of sixty thousand registered physiotherapists; perhaps fifteen percent work in private solo practice, giving roughly nine thousand. Comparable practice-management tools charge between twenty and forty pounds a month, so take thirty, which is three hundred and sixty a year. The full SAM is therefore about three and a quarter million pounds a year. Winning ten percent over five years, itself an ambitious figure against entrenched incumbents, produces around three hundred and twenty-five thousand a year in revenue. That is a viable lifestyle business and an unfundable venture proposition, and knowing that distinction before raising money changes every subsequent decision.

The point of the exercise is not the number itself, which will be wrong. It is to discover the shape of the opportunity and the sensitivity of the outcome to each input. If the business only works at a hundred pounds a month rather than thirty, that becomes a testable pricing assumption. If it only works with fifty percent market share, the plan requires a reason why customers would consolidate on you. Sizing done properly converts a vague ambition into a small number of specific, checkable claims.

sections.heading: Competition and the Rival You Keep Forgetting
sections.body:
Founders routinely answer the competition question with "there is no direct competitor," and mean it as good news. It is almost always either false or bad news. False, because customers are solving the problem somehow today, and whatever they are using is your competition regardless of whether it resembles your product. Bad news, because an empty category usually means others tried and found no money in it, or that the problem is not painful enough to have attracted anyone.

The competitor you must map first is the status quo. For most business problems that means a spreadsheet, a shared inbox, a WhatsApp group, a paper diary, a junior employee doing it manually, or simply tolerating the problem. Doing nothing is the market leader in nearly every category, and it has enormous advantages: it is free, it is already installed, nobody has to be trained on it, no procurement approval is needed, and nobody gets blamed for choosing it. Any new product must overcome not just the functional gap but the switching cost, which includes data migration, retraining, the risk of the new thing failing, and the political cost to whoever championed it.

This is why a widely cited rule of thumb in product strategy holds that a new entrant needs to be several times better on the dimension the customer actually cares about, not marginally better across many dimensions. The Harvard economist John Gourville framed the underlying psychology as the nine-times effect: customers overvalue what they have by roughly three times, innovators overvalue what they have built by roughly three times, and the product of those biases is a nine-fold gap between how good the founder thinks the improvement is and how good it must be to trigger a switch. The specific multiplier is a heuristic rather than a measurement, but the asymmetry it describes is real and repeatedly observed.

Map the landscape in layers. Direct competitors do essentially what you propose. Indirect competitors solve the same underlying job by a different means. Substitutes address the problem by removing it rather than solving it, for instance outsourcing the whole function. And the status quo sits underneath all of them. For each, establish what it costs, what customers complain about, why people choose it, and crucially why people leave it. Public review sites, support forums, app store one- and two-star reviews, and churned-customer interviews are unusually rich sources here, because dissatisfaction is expressed in specific and quotable terms.

Finally, ask what happens when an established player notices you. If your entire advantage is a feature a well-resourced incumbent could ship in a quarter, you have a product, not a business. Durable positions come from distribution, data that compounds, network effects, switching costs you create, regulatory approvals, or serving a segment the incumbent's economics cannot profitably reach.

sections.heading: Smoke Tests, Landing Pages, and Fake Doors
sections.body:
A smoke test presents the offer as though it already exists and measures whether anyone reaches for it. The name comes from hardware engineering, where you power up a new board and see whether smoke comes out. In commercial terms it means building the storefront before the product, and treating the click-through as the measurement.

The simplest version is a landing page describing the product clearly, with a price, and a call to action such as joining a waiting list, requesting a demo or attempting to buy. Traffic is bought deliberately, usually through search or social advertising, so that the audience is strangers with the relevant intent rather than a founder's sympathetic network. That distinction is the whole value of the method: a personal network converts at rates that tell you about your friendships, not your market.

The fake door variant goes further and is more informative. The purchase button is real and leads to a checkout, or a pricing page, and at the final step the visitor is told honestly that the product is not yet available and offered early access. Some teams charge and refund immediately. This produces a genuine intent-to-pay measurement rather than a curiosity measurement, and the gap between the two is usually enormous. It is common to see ten to twenty percent of visitors join a free waiting list and under one percent attempt to pay.

Interpretation requires care and pre-committed thresholds. Decide before you start what result would count as encouraging, discouraging, or ambiguous, and write it down, because deciding afterwards guarantees you will find a way to read whatever you get as encouraging. As rough orientation only, business software landing pages commonly convert visitors to qualified sign-ups somewhere in the range of two to five percent, consumer offers vary far more widely, and figures well outside those ranges deserve investigation rather than celebration. Advertising costs vary by orders of magnitude between categories, so the meaningful number is not the conversion rate alone but the cost per acquired sign-up compared with the revenue you expect that person to generate.

The ethics matter and are frequently handled badly. Taking money for something that does not exist without saying so is fraud in most jurisdictions, and even the softer version leaves people feeling deceived if handled carelessly. Be honest at the point of commitment, tell people plainly that you are testing demand, offer them something real for their trouble such as genuine early access or a discount, and refund promptly and automatically. Handled well, participants often become your first and most engaged customers, because being consulted early creates real goodwill. Handled badly, you burn the small pool of early adopters you will most need later, and in a tight professional community that damage is difficult to undo.

sections.heading: Concierge and Wizard-of-Oz: Delivering by Hand First
sections.body:
Two related techniques let you deliver the actual value to real customers before building anything, and they are consistently underused because they feel like cheating. They are not. They are the fastest way to learn what the product must do.

The concierge method means performing the service manually and openly. The customer knows a human is doing the work. If the eventual product is a meal-planning service, you personally write the plans and email them. If it is an expense-categorization tool, you categorize the expenses by hand each week. Food-kit and personal-styling businesses have repeatedly started this way, and the founders describe the same experience: the first ten customers taught them that half the planned features were irrelevant and that two things they had never considered were the entire point.

The Wizard of Oz method keeps the manual work hidden. The customer sees what appears to be a finished automated product; behind the interface, people are doing the work by hand. The canonical early example is Zappos, where in 1999 Nick Swinmurn photographed shoes in local stores, posted them online, and when an order came in went to the shop, bought the pair at retail and posted it himself. He made no profit and did not care, because the question he was answering was whether people would buy shoes online at all, which in 1999 was genuinely uncertain. Many machine-learning products have followed the same pattern, with humans producing the outputs while the interface and the demand are validated.

Both methods share three strong advantages. They produce real paying customers and therefore real revenue evidence rather than stated intent. They surface the true operational requirements, including the awkward edge cases that no amount of planning reveals. And they let you change the offering weekly at no engineering cost, which is impossible once code exists.

The limits are equally clear. Neither method scales, and it is important to be honest with yourself about the point at which manual delivery is masking an economic problem rather than deferring an engineering one. If the manual version takes four hours per customer per month and the price is thirty pounds, automation must remove almost all of that labour for the business to work, and you should establish early whether it plausibly can. There is also a real ethical line on the hidden variant: it is acceptable to conceal that work is manual, but not to lie if asked directly, and not where the customer's decision depends on it, for instance where they believe sensitive data is being processed by software when in fact a contractor is reading it. Data-protection obligations apply to the humans behind the curtain exactly as they would to a machine.

sections.heading: Pre-selling: The Signal That Outranks Everything Else
sections.body:
There is a hierarchy of evidence in validation, and money at the top of it. Everything else, interest, sign-ups, enthusiasm, survey scores, is a proxy for the question of whether someone will pay. Pre-selling skips the proxy and asks directly. It is uncomfortable, which is exactly why it is informative: the discomfort you feel asking for money is a reasonable measure of how weak you privately suspect the offer to be.

The forms available scale with the customer type. For business-to-business, the ladder runs from a letter of intent, which is non-binding and therefore weak, through a signed pilot agreement with a defined scope and a start date, to a paid pilot with an invoice raised, to a full contract. Each rung costs the buyer more and tells you more. A non-binding letter is worth roughly what it costs to sign, which is nothing; be careful not to build a plan on a stack of them. For consumer products, pre-orders with cards charged, deposits, or a crowdfunding campaign play the same role. Crowdfunding on Kickstarter or a comparable platform is a genuine market test, since it demands that strangers part with money on the strength of a description, and the campaigns that fail to fund have usually learned something true.

Interpret the outcomes carefully, because both directions are informative and both are commonly misread. If people pay, you have learned something powerful but bounded: that this particular offer, at this price, was compelling to this particular group reached through this particular channel. Whether that generalizes to a wider market is a separate question requiring separate evidence, and the classic error is treating twenty enthusiastic early adopters as proof of a mainstream market. Early adopters are systematically unrepresentative; they tolerate rough edges, they enjoy novelty, and they are far easier to sell to than the mainstream that follows.

If people do not pay, resist the reflex conclusion that the idea is dead. Diagnose which link failed. It may be the price, the framing, the specific segment, the channel, the credibility of an unknown seller, the timing within a budget cycle, or the absence of features the buyer treats as mandatory. Ask the people who declined, plainly, what would have had to be different. Refusals interviewed honestly are among the richest data available and almost nobody collects them systematically.

Two practical cautions. First, consumer protection law in most jurisdictions gives buyers cancellation rights and imposes obligations about delivery timelines, and taking pre-orders for something with no realistic delivery date creates genuine legal exposure as well as reputational risk. Second, pre-sale revenue is not free capital; it is a debt denominated in product, and businesses have collapsed under the weight of pre-orders they could not fulfil at the promised price.

sections.heading: Designing a Real Experiment
sections.body:
An experiment that has not been designed in advance will not change anyone's mind, because without a pre-committed threshold every result becomes interpretable as encouragement. The discipline that fixes this is borrowed from science and is not complicated, but it must be written down before any data arrives. The core is a single sentence of the form: we believe a specific thing about a specific group, we will know we are wrong if a specific measurement falls below a specific number within a specific time.

Keep each experiment aimed at exactly one assumption. Tests that bundle demand, price and channel together produce results nobody can interpret, because a failure could have come from any of the three and a success might have come from one carrying the others. Run the cheapest test that could genuinely falsify the belief, not the most impressive one. And commit in advance to what you will do at each outcome, including the unwelcome one, since a decision rule written before the data is the only defence against motivated reasoning afterwards.

Expect most experiments to return an ambiguous result rather than a clean verdict, and plan for that in advance too. An ambiguous outcome usually means the test was aimed at a compound assumption or the sample was too small, and the correct response is to sharpen the question rather than to run the same test again hoping for a friendlier number.
steps: Write the assumption as a falsifiable statement naming a specific population, for example: at least fifteen percent of solo physiotherapists who click a scheduling advert will start a paid trial at thirty pounds a month.
Identify the single riskiest element in that statement. If several things are uncertain at once, split it into separate experiments rather than testing a compound claim.
Choose the cheapest test that could plausibly return a negative result, and be honest about whether a negative result is genuinely possible with the design you have chosen.
Define the metric precisely, including who counts as being in the denominator, so the number cannot be quietly redefined once you see it.
Set the pass, fail and ambiguous thresholds in writing, with dates and a named person recording them, before spending anything.
Decide the sample size needed. For a rough behavioural signal aim for at least one hundred visitors or thirty interviews; smaller samples routinely produce swings that look meaningful and are not.
Set a hard time limit, typically one to three weeks, so an inconclusive test ends rather than drifting on until it produces a comfortable answer.
Run it without interfering. Changing the offer, the copy or the audience partway through destroys the comparison and is the most common way founders spoil their own data.
Record the raw result against the pre-written threshold, before any discussion of what it means.
Decide and document: persevere, pivot the specific element that failed, or stop. Then write the next assumption the result exposed and repeat.

sections.heading: Proving the Money Works: Unit Economics
sections.body:
A business can have delighted customers and still be arithmetically impossible. Unit economics is the discipline of checking whether one customer, considered in isolation, generates more value than they cost to acquire and serve. It is worth doing on the back of an envelope very early, because it frequently disqualifies an idea in twenty minutes.

Four quantities carry most of the meaning. Customer acquisition cost, CAC, is all sales and marketing spend in a period divided by the number of customers acquired in that period, and it must include salaries and agency fees rather than just advertising spend, which is the usual omission. Gross margin is revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the service, including hosting, payment processing at roughly one and a half to three percent, support labour, and any cost of goods. Churn is the fraction of customers who leave each month or year. Lifetime value, LTV, is the gross profit a customer produces before leaving, which for a subscription is roughly the monthly gross profit divided by the monthly churn rate.

Two benchmarks are widely used in subscription software and are useful as orientation rather than law. An LTV to CAC ratio of about three to one is considered healthy; below one the business destroys value with every sale, and much above five often means you are underinvesting in growth. A CAC payback period under twelve months is comfortable for a business funding growth from cash flow, while eighteen to twenty-four months requires external capital to bridge the gap. These figures come from venture-backed software and transfer poorly to other models, so treat them as a sanity check rather than a target.

Work an example. Suppose the price is thirty pounds a month with an eighty percent gross margin, giving twenty-four pounds of monthly gross profit. Suppose monthly churn is five percent, which implies an average customer life of twenty months and an LTV of four hundred and eighty pounds. If advertising delivers a customer for a hundred and sixty pounds all-in, the ratio is three to one and payback is under seven months, which works. Now change churn to ten percent a month, entirely plausible for a small-business tool with weak habit formation. Average life halves to ten months, LTV falls to two hundred and forty, and the ratio drops to one and a half to one, which is marginal. Change CAC to three hundred, which is unremarkable in a competitive advertising auction, and the business is now losing money on every customer it wins.

That sensitivity is the lesson. The outcome swings between viable and fatal on two numbers that founders habitually assume optimistically and rarely test early. Both are testable: churn can be estimated from a paid pilot over three months, and CAC can be estimated from a small advertising spend of a few hundred pounds long before a product exists.

sections.heading: Channel Validation: Can You Reach Them Repeatedly?
sections.body:
An idea can pass every test of desirability and still fail because there is no affordable, repeatable way to reach the people who want it. This is probably the most underweighted risk in the whole exercise. Founders test whether people want the thing, confirm that they do, and never test whether those people can be found at a cost the economics can bear. Distribution is not a detail to be sorted out after the product works; for many businesses it is the business.

The question to answer is specific: through what channel, at what cost per acquired customer, at what volume, and how repeatably? The early sales of almost any venture come through the founder's own network and personal effort, and those sales are systematically misleading. They are cheap because the trust already existed, and they run out. A channel is only validated when a stranger, reached through a mechanism you could run again next month, converts at a cost you can afford.

The realistic options are finite and each has a characteristic profile. Paid advertising on search or social is fast to test and easy to measure, but costs rise as you scale and competitors bid, and it only works where margins are healthy. Content and search-engine optimization is cheap per visitor and compounds well, but takes six to eighteen months to produce meaningful traffic, which is often longer than a new business can survive. Direct outbound sales, cold email and calling, works for higher-priced business products and is highly testable at small scale, but is labour-intensive and constrained by anti-spam law in most jurisdictions. Partnerships and channel resellers can deliver volume but move slowly and shift margin to the partner. Marketplaces and app stores supply distribution in exchange for a substantial cut, commonly fifteen to thirty percent, and control over the customer relationship. Referral and word of mouth is the cheapest and least controllable, and it only works when the product produces genuine enthusiasm.

Test the most plausible one or two early, and test them with real money rather than by reasoning about them. A few hundred pounds of advertising spend against a landing page yields an actual cost per sign-up within a week. Fifty carefully targeted cold emails yields a reply rate within a fortnight. Both numbers are crude, both will change at scale, and both are vastly better than an assumption.

Watch particularly for channel-price mismatch, which is a common and quiet killer. A product priced at fifteen pounds a month cannot support a human sales conversation, because a salesperson costs more per hour than the customer will produce in a year. A product priced at fifty thousand pounds a year rarely sells through self-service advertising, because the buyer requires trust, a procurement process and references. Price and channel must be chosen together, and discovering the mismatch after building is expensive.

sections.heading: Reading Results Honestly: Bias, Noise, and Vanity
sections.body:
Gathering evidence is the easy half. Interpreting it without deceiving yourself is where the discipline is genuinely difficult, because every incentive you have points toward a favourable reading. Founders need conviction to persist, and conviction is corrosive to accurate perception. Naming the specific failure modes helps, because they are recognizable once labelled.

Confirmation bias is the base rate problem: you notice and remember the encouraging conversations and discount the discouraging ones as coming from people who did not understand. A partial defence is to write predictions and thresholds before the data, and to have someone else, ideally a person with no stake, review the raw material rather than your summary of it.

Vanity metrics are numbers that reliably rise and mean nothing. Page views, sign-ups to a free list, social media followers, app downloads, press mentions and waiting-list length all belong here. They feel like progress and they are trivially inflatable. The counterpart, sometimes called actionable metrics, are the ones tied to money and repeated behaviour: activation rate, retention at thirty and ninety days, conversion to paid, revenue per customer, and referral rate. A useful test is to ask whether the number could double without the business being any better off. If it could, it is vanity.

Selection bias contaminates almost all early evidence. The people who answer your outreach, click your advert, or agree to a call are systematically unusual: more interested, more available, more tolerant of novelty. This is not a flaw to be eliminated, since early adopters are your first customers and you need them, but it must be accounted for when generalizing. Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm, published in 1991, is the standard treatment of why the mainstream market behaves so differently from the enthusiasts who precede it, and its central warning has aged well.

Survivorship bias distorts what you learn from other companies. The advice available in books, podcasts and conference talks comes almost entirely from businesses that succeeded, and the same tactics were used by hundreds of failures nobody interviewed. Learning that a famous company ignored its early data proves nothing, because the far larger number who ignored their data and disappeared did not get to write about it.

Finally, beware of small numbers. A test that converts three visitors out of fifty and one out of fifty in two variants has not demonstrated anything; that difference is well within ordinary random variation. Rough behavioural signals need on the order of a hundred or more observations per variant before differences of a few percentage points are worth acting on, and formal significance testing on early startup data is usually false precision applied to a sample far too small to support it.

sections.heading: Pivot, Persevere, or Stop
sections.body:
The point of validation is to reach a decision, and there are only three: continue on the current path, change something substantial, or stop. Founders are reliably good at the first, competent at the second, and extremely bad at the third, which is why the third deserves the most careful thought before emotion is involved.

Persevere when the evidence is genuinely positive on the assumptions you actually tested: the problem surfaces unprompted, people have already spent money or built workarounds, a meaningful fraction converted when asked for a commitment, the arithmetic holds at a plausible price, and you found at least one channel that reached strangers affordably. Note that persevering does not mean the questions stop; it means the next set of assumptions moves to the top of the list.

Pivot when one specific element failed and the rest held. The word has been degraded into a synonym for changing your mind, but it originally meant something more precise: keeping one foot planted while moving the other. Something you learned is worth keeping. Common forms include changing the customer segment while keeping the product, keeping the customer and changing the product, keeping both and changing the pricing model or the channel, and zooming in so that one feature becomes the whole product. That last one has an unusually good track record. Diagnose which link in the chain broke before choosing, because pivoting the wrong element is simply starting over with extra steps and lost time.

Stop when the evidence says the problem is not painful enough, the arithmetic cannot be made to work at any price the market will bear, or no reachable channel exists. Deciding this in advance is the only way it gets done fairly. Write down, before you begin, what result would make you walk away, and give a specific person permission to hold you to it. Set a budget and a deadline, in money and in months, that you will not exceed without a genuine reason rather than a hope. Sunk cost is the enemy here: the correct question is never what you have already spent, which is gone in every scenario, but whether the next pound and the next month are better spent here or elsewhere.

Stopping well is a skill and carries no shame. Close obligations properly, refund anyone owed money promptly, tell the people who helped you what you learned and thank them, and write an honest account of what happened while it is fresh. The relationships and the knowledge survive the venture, and the founders who handle an ending cleanly are the ones people back next time. A validation process that kills three ideas in six months for the price of a modest holiday has done its job perfectly, even though it feels at the time like nothing but a series of disappointments.

guides.title: Conducting Primary Market Research
guides.summary: A complete working guide to primary market research: turning a business decision into a research question, choosing between interviews, surveys, observation and experiments, sampling and sizing, writing questions that do not bias the answer, measuring willingness to pay, analysing the results honestly, and recognising when the research is misleading you.

sections.heading: What Primary Research Is, and When It Is Worth Its Cost
sections.body: Primary market research is the deliberate collection of new evidence, gathered by or for you, about the people whose behaviour determines whether a commercial decision succeeds. It stands in contrast to secondary research, which is the reuse of evidence somebody else already collected: government statistics, industry reports, trade association figures, competitor filings, academic papers. The distinction matters practically rather than philosophically. Secondary evidence is cheap, fast, and almost always the correct first move, because a great deal of what a business wants to know has already been measured by somebody with a bigger budget. Primary research earns its cost only when the question is specific to your situation in a way that no existing dataset can answer: what these particular customers think of this particular product at this particular price. The honest test for whether to commission primary research is the value-of-information test. Ask what decision hangs on the answer, what you would do under each possible answer, and what it would cost to be wrong. If you would launch the product regardless of what customers say, the research is theatre and the money is better spent on the launch. If a plausible finding would genuinely change the decision — kill the feature, halve the price, target a different segment — then the research has option value, and the sensible budget is some fraction of the cost of the mistake it might prevent. A firm considering a three-million-pound factory line can justify a hundred thousand pounds of research. A team choosing between two button colours cannot, and should run a live experiment instead. Primary research divides along two axes that are often confused. The first is qualitative versus quantitative: whether you are trying to discover what the relevant questions and language are, or to measure how common something is among a defined population. The second is stated versus revealed: whether you are asking people what they think and would do, or observing what they actually do. Stated preference is cheap and flexible and systematically optimistic; revealed preference is expensive and narrow and honest. Mature research programmes use qualitative work to generate hypotheses, quantitative surveys to size them, and behavioural experiments to confirm the ones that matter most, in that order. Skipping the qualitative stage produces surveys that measure the researcher's assumptions. Skipping the quantitative stage produces confident generalisation from eight conversations. Skipping the behavioural stage produces launches that miss their forecasts because everyone said they would buy and then did not. Understanding which of these three things you are doing at any moment is the single most useful discipline in the whole field, and the one most frequently abandoned under deadline pressure. A fourth distinction, less often named, separates exploratory from confirmatory work. Exploratory research may wander, change its questions midway, and end with a hypothesis rather than a number. Confirmatory research is a pre-declared test of a stated claim, where changing the analysis after seeing the data destroys its meaning. Reporting exploratory findings as though they had been confirmed is how organisations accumulate confident false beliefs.

sections.heading: From Business Decision to Research Question
sections.body: Most research fails before a single respondent is contacted, at the moment somebody writes a brief saying we want to understand our customers better. That is not a research question; it is a mood. A usable research question is narrow enough that you can imagine the table of results before you collect them, and can say in advance which cell of that table would cause you to act differently. The craft is to walk backwards from the decision. Start by writing the decision in a single sentence with the options enumerated: we will price the subscription at nine, fourteen or nineteen pounds a month. Then list the assumptions on which the choice depends: that demand falls less than proportionally between nine and fourteen; that the fourteen-pound tier does not cannibalise an existing product; that professional users, who are the profitable segment, will not defect at nineteen. Each assumption is a candidate for measurement. Rank them by two criteria: how much the decision changes if the assumption is false, and how uncertain you currently are. The assumptions that are both high-impact and high-uncertainty are what the research should address. Assumptions you are already confident about should be left alone, however interesting; assumptions that do not change the decision should be dropped even if the marketing team is curious. Then translate each surviving assumption into an operational question with a measurable answer. Will professional users defect at nineteen pounds becomes: among users who report more than five hours of weekly professional use, what proportion say they would definitely or probably continue at nineteen pounds a month, and how does that compare with the same figure at fourteen? Notice how much has been forced into the open: the segment definition, the response scale, the comparison. Writing the question this way exposes disagreements early, when they cost nothing, rather than at the debrief. Finally, and most usefully, draft the empty results table and circulate it. Put the segments down the side, the response options across the top, and leave every cell blank. Ask the decision-makers to write in the number they expect, and then to write next to it what they would do if the real number were twenty points lower. This exercise, sometimes called a pre-mortem forecast, does three things at once. It reveals whether the study can actually discriminate between the options on the table. It calibrates the team by exposing how far apart their private expectations are. And it commits people in advance to an interpretation, which makes it much harder for an inconvenient result to be explained away as an artefact of the methodology afterwards. If nobody can name a result that would change their mind, stop and spend the money elsewhere.

sections.heading: Populations, Sampling Frames, and How Samples Go Wrong
sections.body: Every quantitative study is an argument that a small group of people you actually spoke to resembles a large group you care about. Three distinct populations sit inside that argument and confusing them is the commonest fatal error in commercial research. The target population is everyone the conclusion is meant to describe: for instance, all UK households with a combi boiler more than eight years old. The sampling frame is the list or mechanism from which you can actually draw people: a consumer panel, a customer database, footfall at a shopping centre, a mobile advertising audience. The achieved sample is who ultimately responded. Error creeps in at each step. Coverage error is the gap between the target population and the frame. If your frame is your own email list, you have excluded everyone who has never bought from you, which is precisely the group whose opinion determines growth. This is the structural reason that customer-satisfaction surveys chronically overstate a product's appeal: the people most likely to have hated it left and unsubscribed. Sampling error is the random variation from drawing a finite sample out of the frame; it is the only error type that a margin of error actually quantifies, and it shrinks predictably as the sample grows. Non-response error is the difference between those in the frame who answered and those who did not, and it is dangerous precisely because it does not shrink with sample size. A survey with a two per cent response rate and fifty thousand responses can be far more biased than one with a forty per cent response rate and four hundred, because the two per cent who answered are systematically different — more engaged, more aggrieved, more available, more online. The historical cautionary tale is the 1936 Literary Digest poll, which mailed ten million ballots and received 2.4 million back, then confidently predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won 46 states. The sample was enormous and the frame was drawn from telephone directories and car registrations, which in the Depression skewed wealthy and Republican, and the people who bothered to return a ballot skewed further still. George Gallup predicted the result correctly with about fifty thousand quota-sampled interviews. Size did not save the Digest and it will not save you. Practically, this means writing down your frame explicitly and listing who it excludes before you field anything. Then decide between probability sampling, where every member of the frame has a known non-zero chance of selection and statistical inference is formally valid, and non-probability sampling — online panels, quotas, river sampling, convenience intercepts — which is what almost all commercial work actually uses. Non-probability samples can be perfectly serviceable for comparing two concepts, since biases largely cancel in a relative comparison, but they are treacherous for absolute estimates such as market size or penetration. Know which kind of claim you are making.

sections.heading: Sample Size, Margin of Error, and the Arithmetic of Precision
sections.body: Sample size is where research meets budget, and where a little arithmetic prevents a great deal of waste. For a simple proportion — the share of people who say yes — the ninety-five per cent margin of error is approximately 1.96 times the square root of p times one minus p divided by n, where p is the proportion and n the sample size. The expression p(1-p) is largest at p equal to one half, so a conservative rule of thumb is that the margin of error is roughly 0.98 divided by the square root of n. With n equal to 400 that is about plus or minus five percentage points; with 1,000 it is about three; with 2,500 it is about two; with 10,000 it is about one. The crucial feature is the square root. Precision improves with the square root of sample size, so halving the margin of error requires quadrupling the sample and roughly quadrupling the cost. This is why national opinion polls converge on about a thousand respondents: it is the point where further spending buys very little, and where the remaining error is dominated by non-response and weighting rather than by randomness. Spending on 4,000 respondents to move from three points to one and a half is almost always worse value than spending the difference on a better sampling frame or a follow-up behavioural test. Two adjustments matter in commercial work. First, the finite population correction: if you are sampling from a small universe, such as 300 hospital procurement managers, the margin shrinks by a factor of the square root of one minus n over N. Sampling 150 of 300 gives roughly a thirty per cent narrower interval than the naive formula predicts. Second, the design effect: quota sampling, clustering and post-stratification weighting all inflate variance. A design effect of 1.5 means your 1,000 responses behave statistically like about 667. Panel providers can usually supply an effective sample size; ask for it. Sizing should be driven by the smallest subgroup you intend to report on, not by the total. If the decision hinges on professional users who are one in eight of your market, and you need plus or minus seven points on that subgroup, you need roughly 200 professionals and therefore about 1,600 total interviews, or a screened and boosted design that oversamples professionals and re-weights afterwards. Teams routinely field 500 interviews, then slice them into nine segments of about fifty each, and solemnly discuss differences that are pure noise. A difference between two subgroups of fifty needs to be roughly twenty percentage points before it is distinguishable from chance. For qualitative work, the equivalent concept is saturation rather than margin of error. Empirical studies of interview corpora, notably Guest, Bunce and Johnson in 2006, found that most recurrent themes in a reasonably homogeneous group appear within about twelve interviews, with the majority emerging in the first six. Heterogeneous populations need more, typically eight to twelve per distinct segment. There is no formula; you stop when three consecutive interviews teach you nothing structurally new.

sections.heading: Depth Interviews: Structure, Guides, and Laddering
sections.body: The one-to-one depth interview is the workhorse of exploratory research, and it is far harder than it looks because the natural human instinct in conversation is to be agreeable. A respondent who senses what you want to hear will supply it, not out of dishonesty but out of ordinary social cooperation. Nearly every technique in interviewing exists to defeat that instinct. Interviews run on a discussion guide rather than a script: a sequence of topics with a few prepared probes, deliberately loose enough that the respondent can lead you somewhere you did not anticipate. A typical sixty-minute guide allocates five minutes to rapport and context, ten to the respondent's current behaviour in their own words, twenty-five to the core topic, ten to reactions to any stimulus such as a concept board, and ten to closing and anything the respondent thinks you have missed. Open with grand-tour questions: walk me through the last time you did this; what happened just before that. Concrete, recent, specific episodes produce reliable recall. Questions about what people generally do, or would do, produce self-image rather than behaviour. The single most valuable habit is to ask about the last time rather than about typical behaviour, and to chase the story until it is anchored in verifiable detail: which day, who else was there, what it cost, what nearly went wrong. A second habit is silence. After an answer, wait three full seconds. Respondents almost always continue, and the continuation is usually more candid than the first answer, which was the socially rehearsed one. A third is to reflect back in the respondent's own vocabulary rather than paraphrasing into corporate language, because the moment you say so you value convenience you have supplied a frame they will adopt. Laddering, developed out of Gutman's means-end chain theory in the early 1980s, is the structured technique for getting from surface attributes to underlying values. You take a stated preference — I like that it is stainless steel — and ask why that matters to you, repeatedly, typically four to six times. Stainless steel becomes it does not stain, becomes it still looks new after years, becomes I do not feel like I bought something cheap, becomes I want my home to say I am competent. The terminal answers are values, and they are what advertising and positioning actually address; the opening answers are attributes, and they are what engineering addresses. Both are useful, but confusing them produces campaigns that recite specifications to people who are buying self-respect. Guard against three failure modes. Leading questions, which contain the answer, should be replaced with neutral alternatives: not did the price seem high but how did the price strike you. Hypothetical questions, which invite invention, should be replaced with historical ones. And moderator drift, where the interviewer gradually adopts the respondent's assumptions across a long day, should be caught by reviewing your own recordings periodically rather than trusting your memory of how you asked.

sections.heading: Focus Groups and the Physics of Group Dynamics
sections.body: A focus group is six to eight strangers, a moderator, ninety minutes and a topic. It was popularised in the 1940s by the sociologist Robert Merton, who studied wartime radio propaganda responses, and it became the default qualitative instrument of the advertising industry from the 1960s onward. It is simultaneously the most familiar and the most misused method in the field, because group settings do something specific and limited well, and something else very badly. What groups do well is generate range and language. When one person names an irritation, others recognise it and elaborate, producing vocabulary and edge cases that no individual would have volunteered cold. Groups are excellent for exploring how a category is talked about, for surfacing social norms, and for stress-testing a proposition against sceptics in real time. They are also efficient: eight opinions in ninety minutes rather than eight hours. What groups do badly is measure anything, and produce independent judgements. Two well-documented effects dominate. Social conformity, demonstrated in Solomon Asch's line-judgement experiments in the 1950s where roughly a third of responses conformed to an obviously wrong majority, means individual opinions migrate toward the group's apparent consensus. Group polarisation means that a group's average position after discussion is typically more extreme in the initially favoured direction than the average of its members beforehand. Add one confident, articulate participant and the session can become a transcript of that person's views with seven people nodding. Never treat counts from a focus group — five out of eight liked it — as data. They are not a sample of anything. Practical countermeasures are well established. Collect private written responses before any discussion of a stimulus, so you have uncontaminated first reactions on paper; the divergence between the private forms and the subsequent conversation is itself informative. Recruit for homogeneity within a group and heterogeneity between groups, because mixing a senior buyer with a junior user suppresses the junior voice entirely. Use at least three or four groups per segment, since any single group develops its own idiosyncratic dynamic. Seat the moderator so they can see everyone, and explicitly invite the quiet participants by name at intervals. Recruitment quality determines everything else. Professional respondents who attend groups weekly for the incentive give fluent, performed, useless answers; reputable recruiters screen for anyone who has participated in the last six months and verify screening answers by telephone rather than by form. Screeners should never reveal the client or category in a way that lets a respondent tailor their answers to qualify. And be sceptical of the viewing room: executives watching through the glass tend to remember the vivid articulate participant and forget the boring representative one, which is precisely backwards. Insist that any conclusion drawn in the viewing room be re-tested against the full transcripts before it enters a decision.

sections.heading: Observation, Ethnography, and Contextual Inquiry
sections.body: People are unreliable narrators of their own behaviour, not because they lie but because much of what they do is habitual, unremarkable and therefore unmemorable. Ask someone how they clean their kitchen and you will get a tidy, rational account. Watch them and you will see them use the same cloth for four surfaces, abandon a product because the cap sticks, and improvise a solution with a butter knife. Observational methods exist to capture the gap between the account and the act. Ethnography in a commercial setting usually means an in-context visit of two to four hours in the home, workplace or vehicle where the behaviour actually happens. The researcher watches, asks the participant to narrate as they go, photographs the environment with permission, and takes an inventory: what is actually in the cupboard, what is half-used, what is stored where. Physical evidence is powerful because it is unfaked. A stated loyalty to a premium brand alongside a cupboard of supermarket own-label is a more informative finding than any answer to a loyalty question. Contextual inquiry, formalised by Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt in the 1990s for software design, structures this into a master-apprentice relationship. The participant is the master doing their real work; the researcher is the apprentice who watches and asks why at natural pauses rather than interrupting. Its four principles are context, meaning go to the place; partnership, meaning avoid both the interview and the expert stance; interpretation, meaning share your reading aloud so the participant can correct it in the moment; and focus, meaning keep a clear question in mind so a four-hour visit does not become undirected tourism. Related techniques trade depth for scale. Diary studies ask participants to log events as they occur, increasingly via a phone app with photographs and timestamps, over one to four weeks; they capture infrequent or embarrassing behaviours that a single visit would miss, at the cost of participant fatigue after about ten days. Mystery shopping and service safaris put a trained observer through the customer journey to record what actually happens rather than what the process manual says. Shelf and footfall observation in retail records dwell time, path and pick-up-and-replace behaviour, which correlates far better with purchase than recalled attention does. Usage data and instrumentation, where you can ethically obtain it, is observation at industrial scale. The characteristic weaknesses are also worth stating plainly. Observation is expensive per participant, so sample sizes are tiny and generalisation is unwarranted. The observer effect is real: people tidy up, perform competence, and use products more carefully when watched, an effect that decays over the first twenty to thirty minutes, which is why visits should be long. And analysis is labour-intensive; a three-hour visit generates several hours of transcription and coding. Budget roughly two to three hours of analysis for every hour in the field, or the material will sit unwatched on a hard drive and the study will collapse into whatever the researcher happens to remember.

sections.heading: Writing Survey Questions That Do Not Lie to You
sections.body: A survey is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument it can be miscalibrated. The unsettling finding from decades of survey methodology is that question wording routinely moves answers by ten to thirty percentage points, which is far larger than the sampling error everyone frets about. Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer's 1974 experiment showed that asking how fast cars were going when they smashed into each other produced speed estimates about nine miles per hour higher than when they hit each other, and made witnesses more likely to falsely recall broken glass. Every principle below descends from that basic fragility. Ask about one thing at a time. Double-barrelled items such as how satisfied are you with the speed and accuracy of delivery cannot be answered by anyone who is happy with one and not the other, and the resulting number means nothing. Split them. Use the respondent's vocabulary, not the organisation's: nobody outside the company knows what onboarding or omnichannel means, and respondents will guess rather than admit confusion. Avoid negation, and never use double negation; do you disagree that the service should not be discontinued is a trap even for careful readers. Balance the response options. Offering excellent, very good, good, fair, poor is not a scale, it is an invitation, because four of the five options are positive. A balanced five-point scale has two positive, one neutral and two negative options with symmetric labels. Decide deliberately whether to include a midpoint — omitting it forces a lean and slightly increases apparent polarisation — and whether to offer an explicit don't know, which reduces the manufacture of opinions about things respondents have never considered. Randomise the order of long option lists to defuse primacy effects, which are strong in visual self-completion and reverse into recency effects when options are read aloud on the telephone. Beware of acquiescence bias, the general human tendency to agree, which inflates agree-disagree batteries by roughly ten per cent and hits lower-education and some cultural groups harder. The standard remedy is item-specific response formats — how easy or difficult was it, with labelled endpoints — rather than strings of agree-disagree statements. Include a few reverse-worded items to detect straightlining, where a respondent selects the same option down a whole grid. Add at least one attention check, but a fair one: a screening item with an obviously correct answer, not a trick. Finally, mind ordering and context. Questions prime the ones that follow, so ask general questions before specific ones, and place sensitive demographics at the end when rapport is established. Always pilot: run the draft with ten to twenty people using think-aloud cognitive interviewing, where the respondent narrates their interpretation as they answer. A pilot of twenty takes a day and routinely uncovers two or three questions that respondents were reading in a way the author never imagined.

sections.heading: Fielding a Survey: Modes, Response Rates, and Procedure
sections.body: Mode — how the questionnaire reaches people — shapes both cost and answers. Online self-completion dominates commercial work because it is cheap, fast, supports images and complex logic, and removes the social pressure that inflates socially desirable answers. Its weakness is coverage and engagement: panel members are unrepresentative in ways that weighting only partially fixes, and completion quality decays sharply past about twelve minutes. Telephone interviewing reaches populations that are offline, allows probing, and achieves better representativeness, but costs perhaps ten to twenty times as much per interview and reintroduces interviewer effects. Face-to-face is the gold standard for representativeness and the only realistic option in low-connectivity markets, at the highest cost. Intercept surveys at a location capture people in the moment of the behaviour, at the price of a frame that is nothing but that location. Response rates have collapsed over four decades. Telephone response rates that were above sixty per cent in the 1980s are now frequently under ten per cent, and unsolicited email survey rates of two to five per cent are ordinary. Since non-response bias does not shrink with sample size, the useful levers are the ones that raise response: brevity, a credible and specific explanation of purpose, a named sender, a guaranteed unconditional incentive rather than a prize draw, and at least two reminders. Don Dillman's tailored design method, refined since 1978, consistently shows that multiple contacts and a modest prepaid incentive outperform a large conditional one. Watch fieldwork daily rather than waiting for the closing report, because most fatal problems are visible in the first fifty completes and cheap to fix then.
steps: Define the target population and the screening criteria precisely, then write the screener questions that operationalise them without revealing what qualifies a respondent.
Choose the mode and the sample source, and obtain from the provider the incidence rate, expected length of interview, effective sample size and cost per complete before committing.
Draft the questionnaire against the decision table, keeping median completion under twelve minutes online; time it yourself and cut the questions nobody would act on.
Programme the survey with routing, quotas and quality traps, then test every logical path yourself, including the paths that should terminate a respondent.
Run a soft launch of roughly ten per cent of the sample, typically fifty to a hundred completes, and pause automatically at that threshold.
Interrogate the soft-launch data: check drop-off by question, straightlining rates, median time per page, open-text coherence, and whether any quota is filling far faster than expected.
Fix problems and, if the questionnaire changed materially, discard the soft-launch responses rather than pooling them with the main wave.
Release the full field, monitor quota fill daily, and send reminders on day three and day seven to non-responders where the sample source permits.
Close the field on schedule rather than extending it to chase a target, since late responders differ systematically from early ones and extending changes the sample composition.
Clean the data: remove speeders below roughly one third of median time, straightliners, failed attention checks and duplicate fingerprints, and document exactly how many cases each rule removed.

sections.heading: Measuring Willingness to Pay
sections.body: Price is the single most leveraged variable in most businesses and the one people answer least honestly about, because the socially easy answer to would you pay more is no. Directly asking what would you pay for this produces a number that is systematically low and weakly related to behaviour. Four structured techniques exist to do better, each with a distinct failure profile. The Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter, published in 1976, asks four questions about the same product: at what price would it be so cheap you would doubt its quality; so expensive you would not consider it; expensive but still worth considering; and a bargain. Plotting the cumulative curves gives intersections conventionally read as an acceptable range and an optimal price point. It is cheap and it reliably identifies a plausible corridor, but it measures perceived value in the abstract with no competitive context and no volume information, so it cannot forecast revenue. Treat its output as a sanity check, never as a recommendation. Gabor-Granger presents a single price and asks purchase likelihood, then walks the price up or down through a ladder, building a demand curve from which revenue at each price can be computed. It gives volume as well as acceptability, which Van Westendorp does not, but it is transparently about price, so respondents can perform bargain-hunting. It also assumes your product exists in isolation. Discrete choice modelling, usually called conjoint analysis, is the most rigorous of the standard methods. Respondents see repeated sets of three or four competing product profiles that vary simultaneously in price, brand, features and other attributes, and simply choose one or none. Because price never appears alone, the respondent cannot game it; the trade-offs they make reveal the implicit utility of each attribute level. Fitting a multinomial logit or hierarchical Bayes model yields part-worth utilities per respondent, from which you can simulate share and revenue for any hypothetical market configuration, including a competitor's response. The cost is complexity: a good design needs a defensible attribute list from prior qualitative work, typically eight to twelve choice tasks per respondent, three hundred or more respondents, and a specialist to build and validate it. Its main weakness is that it measures preference among presented options in a simplified world without shelf clutter, credit constraints or inertia, and so overstates switching. The strongest evidence is always behavioural. A live price test — genuinely charging different prices to randomly assigned visitors, or running a pre-order at a real price where money actually changes hands — beats every stated-preference method. The classic honest compromise, when a live test is impossible, is to combine conjoint with a calibration factor derived from a past launch where both the research forecast and the actual outcome are known. Typical calibration ratios in consumer goods run between 0.4 and 0.7 of stated intent, meaning roughly half of the people who said they would definitely buy did not.

sections.heading: Experiments and Causal Inference in the Field
